articles.title: Dine and dashers hiding plastic in food, and not paying bills
articles.summary: Pubs and restaurants describe how they have been targeted by customers trying to avoid paying.
articles.body:
Restaurants and pubs have reported hundreds of incidents of customers running off without paying to Devon and Cornwall Police in recent years. The force said it remained an under reported crime and warned businesses who have been victims off creating their own appeals on social media.

We have been to Newlyn in Cornwall to talk to publicans and restaurateurs about their experiences with dine and dash, and how they have dealt with it.

"We had a family who planted plastic in their piece of bread and then pretended they had chipped their tooth biting into it," said Nina Maclean from Mackerel Sky Seafood Bar in the town in recent years.

As well as capturing customers on CCTV planting objects like plastic and hair in their food, others have run away without paying.

After one such incident, Maclean tried to locate the offenders on social media.

"Afterwards, the couple did call us to ask if we could remove their faces from social media and we said we'll happily remove the post if they pay the bill which they refused to do - ultimately it's theft," she said.

"I don't think there is a lot the police can do, which is a shame because then it doesn't discourage people from doing it, but you just have to hope that people are going to be honest, and the majority of people are honest and decent."

Devon and Cornwall Police urged more businesses to send in evidence when incidents happen, instead of using social media to try and track down the culprits.

Other restaurants and pubs have also used social media to track down people who have run off without paying.

Just set back from the bustling fishing harbour, general manager of The Swordfish pub Trevelyan Worth said customers had walked out without paying bills £140 and £380 in the last year.

After posting about the incidents on social media, one customer did eventually pay their bill, but the other one remains unresolved.

"The highest damage aside from the finance is trust," he said.

"You go into a lot of businesses these days and you are expected to pay up front. I still operate on trust."

A few hundred metres away, overlooking the port, the Fisherman's Arms has also had experience with dine and dashers.

Co-owner Nicholas George, who also owns The Logan Rock Inn near Porthcurno and two pubs on the Isles of Scilly, said: "We've had four or five events and we've traced them down through social media and they have paid every single time."

Now he asks people to pay when ordering if they are sitting outside, or if his staff do do not know the customer.

Customers eating and then making off without paying affects a third of restaurants, according to UK Hospitality.

Sgt Chris Chaloner from Devon and Cornwall Police said it was a criminal offence if somebody has eaten at a restaurant, and then deliberately left without paying.

He admitted the force does not have enough intelligence around the issue as rates of reported incidents have not been high.

Figures obtained by a freedom of information request by the BBC show there have been 234 reports from hospitality businesses to Devon and Cornwall Police since 2022, of customers making off without paying.

In total, when including all outlets like petrol stations and shops this figure rises to 2,802.

Chaloner said: "It's theft and we should be dealing with that. My advice would be to not to put anything out on social media, report to the police, send us the evidence and we'll do the rest."

Temporary Ch Supt Antony Hart also urged victims to speak to the police.

He said: "Once an image is posted online it's almost impossible to fully remove, and there is a risk that individuals may be wrongly identified.

"This can cause significant distress to innocent people and their families. Extra care should also be taken where children or young people may be captured in footage or images.

"Publishing images before police inquiries have been completed can also affect an investigation. It may influence potential witnesses, impact formal identification procedures, or alert suspects to police interest, which can make inquiries more challenging.

"Where there is a genuine investigative need to seek the public's help in identifying someone, police can release images in a controlled and lawful way, in line with national guidance and legislation."

articles.title: Bags still missing for passenger after air traffic control chaos
articles.summary: A passenger from Surrey waits for her bags after her flight is among thousands to be cancelled.
articles.body:
A passenger who had to abandon her holiday due to an air traffic control technical issue says she has still not had her baggage returned a week later.

Helen Moore from Ottershaw, Surrey, abandoned her holiday to Corfu after a nine-hour wait at Heathrow Airport when her flight was caught up in widespread cancellations earlier in September.

She told BBC Radio Surrey that British Airways had not returned her luggage and she had received "really no good information at all" until Monday.

British Airways said last Wednesday it was "incredibly sorry" for the experience customers endured "because of an issue that has been entirely out of our control".

Heathrow's operations have returned to normal and the airport is directing luggage inquiries to airlines.

Hundreds of thousands of people are thought to have been affected across two days of travel chaos after the air traffic control system operated by Nats went down for four hours on 8 September.

Nats previously said it was investigating the glitch and apologised for the fault - the third major issue in as many years.

Moore said the situation in Terminal 5 had been "absolute chaos" and she found passengers "were just milling around with no luggage" after she disembarked the plane.

"There was some baggage on the carousel, a lot of bags, but they were all mixed up," she said.

"They weren't just off one particular flight, there were no signs up saying where the bags would be."

She added: "We took the decision very early on that it was better to be at home with no luggage than away on holiday with no luggage."

Moore's holiday has been refunded but she remains without her luggage, which contained her husband's hearing aids and spare glasses.

"He won't be doing that again, but that's on him," she said.

According to the UK Civil Aviation Authority, airlines are liable for lost or damaged baggage but there are "no rules which fix the amount of compensation you should receive".

The organisation advises passengers that it "might be better to claim on your travel insurance" as airlines "may not pay out the true cost" of delays or lost luggage.

articles.title: Afghan inquiry into alleged SAS war crimes has already cost £58m, MOD figures show
articles.summary: The inquiry has been running for more than three and a half years but has yet to publish any findings.
articles.body:
An inquiry into allegations British Special Forces murdered unarmed Afghan civilians has cost UK taxpayers £58m, figures from the Ministry of Defence (MoD) show.

When the inquiry was launched in 2023, its chair Lord Justice Haddon-Cave said it would aim to report, "at least on an interim basis", within 12-18 months.

However, the inquiry has now been running for more than three and a half years, and has yet to publish any findings.

In a statement, the inquiry said its work was "greater and more complex than it originally envisaged".

It added that delays by the MoD in disclosing information had also affected the timetable.

The Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan (IIRTA) was established to investigate alleged war crimes committed by soldiers serving with the Special Air Service between 2010 and 2013, during so called night raids targeting the Taliban.

These include allegations the SAS murdered detainees and unarmed civilians, including children, during operations.

It was set up by the former defence secretary, Ben Wallace, in the wake of allegations first reported by BBC Panorama, in 2022.

SAS unit repeatedly killed Afghan detainees, BBC finds

SAS had golden pass to get away with murder, inquiry told

SAS war crime evidence suppressed, inquiry hears

While much of the inquiry's work has been carried out in closed sessions to protect the identities of serving personnel, it has published some evidence on its website.

It has already heard evidence from senior UK military personnel who have said they believed the SAS carried out extra judicial killings of Afghan civilians.

It has also heard concerns about the secrecy in which the SAS operated and that previous investigations into the allegations were ended prematurely.

The inquiry's costs were £14.68m, until the end of the 2024-5 financial year. Those included the salary of the chair, Sir Charles Haddon-Cave, its secretariat, lawyers and expert witnesses. The inquiry said its expenditure was proportionate and overseen judicially.

However, the Ministry of Defence has given a much higher figure. Following a Freedom of Information request submitted by the BBC, the MoD put the overall cost at £58m to March 2026.

The figure included the costs to the MoD as well as those of the inquiry team, it said. The MoD said that 74 of its staff were currently working more than 50% of their time on the inquiry.

The SAS Regimental Association (SASRA), which represents more than 5,000 SAS veterans and serving personnel, said it remained committed to supporting the inquiry and helping achieve a "timely solution".

But in a statement, it added: "The prolonged nature of the process is itself causing significant and widening harm."

It said the inquiry posed a "significant challenge, not only to the regiment's reputation and the wellbeing and morale of its members, but in the association's view, to the operational effectiveness of a key element of the nation's defence".

It said the cumulative effect of decades of legal scrutiny arising from operations in Northern Ireland, Iraq, Afghanistan and Syria was placing a significant burden on individuals, families and the association itself.

Public inquiries are rarely quick or cheap. The Bloody Sunday Inquiry, which found the killing of 13 civil rights protesters in Northern Ireland by British soldiers was "unjustified", took 12 years to complete and cost more than £190m.

In response, the inquiry said it remained committed to the welfare and safety of UK Special Forces personnel, and a timely conclusion to the inquiry was in everyone's interest.

"The chair remains committed to the welfare and safety of UK Special Forces personnel and witnesses who come forward to the inquiry."

articles.title: Australia immigration crackdown: visas for international students and backpackers targeted
articles.summary: The government wants to reduce net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.
articles.body:
International students, so-called "visa hoppers" and backpackers will be targeted under stricter rules announced by Australia on Thursday in a bid to curb immigration.

Foreign students will no longer be able to bring their families with them and those who want to extend their stay must choose a higher qualification.

Rules will also be stricter for working holiday visas - commonly used by backpackers and a crucial labour source for the agricultural sector - with a ballot system although these changes will not affect the UK.

The new rules were revealed by Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke who said that while immigration was a "strength" of Australia, there needed to be a "high level of control".

For international student and graduate visas, Burke said: "We will no longer be adding to the stock of students automatically being able to bring family members over."

There would be exemptions for foreign students already in Australia as well as applicants from the Pacific and South East Asian countries, he said.

PhD students would also be able to bring their families as they were in different life circumstances to undergraduates, Burke said.

In a speech titled "The work of managing the migration program: who arrives, who stays, who leaves", Burke revealed a raft of changes as the government aims to bring net overseas migration to 225,000 people by 2028.

On student visas, he said the government would clamp down on "visa hopping" - where a student finishes a course, then applies to do another course which is often a lower qualification and sometimes with a "not so legitimate provider".

Students who want to go "up the scale" will be allowed, Burke said, for example, if a student finishes a bachelor's degree and then wants to complete a masters.

He also announced major changes to working holiday visas for those aged 18 to 30 years old who can work in Australia for 12 months, but can extend for a second and third year.

Currently, these visa holders must work for three months in regional Australia during their first year to qualify for a second year, and then six months to qualify for a third year.

Under the new changes, those who qualify for a second year will have to go into a ballot with a cap of 45,000, down from the 57,000 who qualified last year.

For the third year, the ballot will be limited to 5,000, down from 31,000 who qualified last year. British working holidaymakers will not be affected by these changes due to the UK's free trade agreement with Australia.

New figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday showed Australia's population grew 1.4% in the 12 months to March 2026 to 27.9m.

That total figure included births and deaths as well as a net overseas migration of 292,100.

Migration remains a major political issue as debate around Australia's population grows amid rising living costs, housing affordability and increased strain on public services.

One Nation, a populist right-wing party known for its anti-immigration stance and which has seen a surge in support in recent months, detailed its migration policy earlier this week, proposing to cut temporary migrant visas by 750,000 over three years.

The party, which won its first lower house seat in May , also wants to cap net overseas immigration to 130,000, drawing a rebuke from Burke who said such a proposal would risk "smashing parts of the Australian economy".

In July, the government introduced a policy to prioritise applications for family visas lodged onshore - where the applicant is in the country already - over those submitted overseas.

Skilled migrants already in Australia who applied for permanent visas were also prioritised over those applying from overseas.

It also paused applications for working holiday visas from 24 countries, not including the UK.

Violet Roumeliotis, from Settlement Services International which helps new arrivals to Australia, says the migration debate was increasingly driven by "short-term politics rather than what is best for the country".

"The proposed changes to family visas for international students is a good example of this," she said, adding that it would make it harder for Australia to compete for "future talent".

articles.title: Rare tree offspring given lifeline at Logan Botanic Gardens
articles.summary: Logan Botanic Garden is helping save a species native to Robinson Crusoe Island in the South Pacific.
articles.body:
The offspring of one of the world's rarest trees has been given a new home in south-west Scotland as conservationists step up efforts to save the species from extinction.

Two seedlings from the last known wild dendroseris neriifolia tree have arrived at Logan Botanic Garden in Dumfries and Galloway after an international rescue effort involving experts in Chile and the UK.

The species, native to Robinson Crusoe Island in the South Pacific, has been pushed to the brink by habitat loss, invasive species and repeated wildfires.

Conservationists hope the move will provide a vital safeguard for the future of a plant that now survives in the wild as a single tree clinging to a cliff face.

Garden's sapphire tower flower begins to bloom

Giant plants make epic journey to new home

The dendroseris neriifolia, a rare tree daisy found only on Chile's Robinson Crusoe Island, has suffered a dramatic decline over recent decades.

By 1980, only eight wild specimens remained, and although reintroduction projects were launched in the early 2000s, the breakdown of protection measures in 2017 left the species vulnerable once again to invasive plants and grazing animals.

Today, the last surviving wild tree is supported by ropes on a steep volcanic outcrop to prevent it from falling.

In May this year, 29 seeds were collected from the lone tree and sent to the Millennium Seed Bank at Kew Wakehurst.

Eight seedlings successfully germinated, with two now transferred to Logan Botanic Garden, where the climate is considered particularly suitable for rare Chilean plants. The remaining seedlings will stay at Kew.

Richard Baines, curator at Logan, described the arrival as a significant moment and said the garden could play an important role in learning more about the species and helping secure its future.

"Experience shows that plant species from the Juan Fernández Islands do well at Logan," he said.

"This is the start of an exciting new period.

"Creating a safe place for these seedlings, getting to know them, and learning more about their adaption to different environments, gives us the chance to contribute so much more."

Scientists involved in the project said the international collaboration offered a rare opportunity to prevent the extinction of a unique plant lineage and preserve part of the natural heritage of the Juan Fernández archipelago.

Diego Penneckamp, a scientist at Jardín Botánico VerdeNativo, said saving the species was a "race against time".

"This international collaboration to support the last remaining individual could prevent the extinction of a species that represents a unique lineage with its own natural history," he said.

articles.title: Guernsey, Jersey and Isle of Man issue smart glasses warning
articles.summary: Officials say there are benefits to the technology, but urged users to be mindful when recording.
articles.body:
Islanders are being warned about the "considerable privacy risks" in recording using smart glasses.

The Isle of Man, Jersey and Guernsey's data protection authorities have teamed up to warn that the discreet and wearable technology could capture conversations and personal information without people knowing.

Officials said smart glasses were "increasingly" being used, including in workplaces and businesses. Paul Vane, Jersey Information Commissioner, said there were "benefits" to the technology, but warned "there are also considerable privacy risks".

The authorities have urged users to be "mindful and respectful" and consider when recording is appropriate.

Vane said people affected must feel able to exercise their statutory rights under data protection laws.

"And feel empowered to challenge users who have not been transparent about the use of the technology," Vane added.

Dr Alexandra Delaney-Bhattacharya, Isle of Man Information Commissioner, said the technology could "open up the world" for people with "disabilities especially".

"But the same features that make them useful also make them easy to misuse," she said.

"We know from experience that women and girls are disproportionately the ones filmed without consent, whether by a stranger on the street or someone at a party.

"It takes only a glance to record someone, and that footage can end up anywhere including with a company beyond our shores.

"Our message is simple: think before you share, and ask yourself how you'd feel, or how a woman in your life would feel, if it were her in that footage."

articles.title: Bluefin tuna permits could create 'amazing Guernsey fishery'
articles.summary: The States is due to debate whether to allow catch and release of tuna in Guernsey later this year.
articles.body:
Guernsey has the potential to be "one of the best game fisheries on the planet" should a ban on catching bluefin tuna be lifted, an angler has said.

Landing bluefin tuna is currently prohibited in Guernsey, both commercially and recreationally.

The Committee for Economic Development is putting forward proposals to introduce a permit system for recreational bluefin tuna fishing, on a catch-and-release basis, to be debated later this year.

A local marine biologist has warned important steps need to be undertaken in Guernsey's existing fisheries, before the island moved to allow bluefin fishing.

Former angling journalist and angler Greg Whitehead said he first saw bluefin tuna in Guernsey waters in 2017.

He said that, since then, their numbers had increased drastically.

He said: "There's thousands and thousands of fish out there anytime from mid-June, all the way through to into the new year.

"There's massive potential this is one of the best game fisheries on the planet. I'm not sure anybody would ever expect to say that of the English Channel."

The call comes after five new licences were granted to fishermen to catch and kill bluefin tuna in Jersey.

They were granted as part of new commercial and scientific bluefin tuna trials which will use 26 tonnes of the UK's 2026 bluefin tuna quota and operate in Wales, Jersey and Scotland.

The International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) manages and monitors the capture of bluefin tuna by allocating catch quotas to countries and regions it has a contracting party with.

The UK has been a contracting party since 2020.

In order for Guernsey anglers to obtain recreational permits for bluefin tuna fishing, the UK's contracting party status to ICCAT must be extended to include the bailiwick, along with a raft of other legislative changes to ensure Guernsey meets the necessary compliance requirements.

Then, in principle, Guernsey anglers could be offered a share of the UK quota, which Whitehead said did not need to be significant and "just a few tonnes would be enough to licence dozens of recreational vessels".

He added, however, the obstacle was not just obtaining the quota, but the condition of existing fisheries management in Guernsey, which he said was "failing".

Nicky Harris, marine biology section lead at La Société Guernesiaise, agreed that, while it might be tempting to immediately follow Jersey, Guernsey's fisheries were in nowhere near the same position.

"Guernsey, in comparison, is very under resourced for monitoring and enforcement... The fishermen in Guernsey acutely feel this - this lack of care for marine health," she said.

Harris said, while not against the introduction of a tuna fishery, it was not a "fix-all" solution to an already declining industry.

She said: "It's almost being seen as a band-aid, a sticking plaster, instead of actually looking at improving the wider health of our marine waters through more effective management measures.

"[Tuna fishing] has to be evidence-led, it has to be well managed, it has to be sustainably managed. But we don't see at that point that that's going to happen."

The Economic Development Department has been contacted for a comment.

articles.title: Bristol fashion business 'shocked' at Dragon's Den investment
articles.summary: The ethical fashion start-up caught the eye of Dragon's Den investor Deborah Meaden.
articles.body:
A business owner has said he was "completely shocked" after being offered more money than he was asking for on the BBC's Dragons' Den.

Sam Mabley, from Bristol, founded the sustainable fashion company Yes Friends in 2021 and was approaching the dragons to ask for £10,000 in exchange for a 2% share of the business.

Yes Friends, which says it seeks to "transform the fashion industry" by creating affordable, ethical and sustainable clothing, caught the eye of Deborah Meaden, who offered Mabley double what he was asking for in exchange for the same share.

"I was completely shocked, I didn't know what to say," said Mabley.

"After the den I was like 'I'm pretty sure that's never happened' and she was like 'I don't think that's ever happened before'," he added.

Yes Friends create clothes for men and women using organic Fairtrade cotton. It pays textile workers in India a fair wage and allows customers to tip them through its website.

The company says it only costs an extra "15p to 20p per T-shirt" to pay the workers a living wage, meaning they are able to keep retail prices low and create a better environment for workers in an industry where low pay, poor conditions and exploitation are common.

"It might be more sustainable to make them in Bedminster [where the company is based], but if we're going to make it affordable as well, then it's much easier to produce abroad," Mabley told BBC Points West.

Mabley's pitch also drew the attention of dragon Touker Suleyman, but ultimately it was Meaden's offer of extra cash and her experience working with ethical businesses that won through.

"I have got the absolute audience that you are talking to and I really want to be your investor," she said.

Mabley said the pitch was "terrifying" but having the Dragon on board was "exciting" and could bring "wisdom and experience" to his company.

The business plans to invest the money in new stock that can open it up to new audiences.

Mabley says the business is also looking at ways to "increase the impact we have for garment workers".

Dr Emma Rigby, associate director of the fashion department at the University of the West of England, said: "Fairtrade and organic cotton provide some examples of better practice in the production and manufacture of cotton, yet when considering sustainability, these matters are more complicated."

She said growing cotton always uses a lot of water, but doing it organically is "no doubt better for the environment".

But organic cotton can cause supply issues for farmers, she said, due to the potential for significantly smaller yields.

Rigby said the Fairtrade approach was "incredibly valuable" because of the protections for farmers and workers in an industry that "generates significant profit through the exploitation of both people and resources".

She added: "A sustainable clothing item is one with a local and light production footprint, one that is thoughtfully made, valued by its owner, and cherished and worn well."

articles.title: Alex Batty's new life and job since he was abducted by his mother
articles.summary: Alex Batty, who vanished aged 11 in 2017, says a new job has given him renewed purpose.
articles.body:
Alex Batty, who disappeared for six years after being abducted by his mother as a child, has described feeling a renewed "sense of purpose" after finding work.

Batty, from Oldham, was declared missing by his grandmother in 2017, aged 11, after his mother and grandfather failed to return him from a holiday in Spain and instead moved to France

Batty, who is now 20, said his job at a waste management company had given his young family financial security.

It has been a whirlwind couple of years for Batty, whose teenage years were spent living as a nomad in France.

His mother, Melanie, who was not his legal guardian and was heavily influenced by conspiracy theories, told him to throw away his passport.

They lived off-grid and he did not attend school.

When he was discovered, he was heading for Toulouse with just a skateboard and €100 in cash.

Alex returned to live with his grandmother Susan Caruana, his legal guardian, in Oldham shortly afterwards, but found himself out of work for a long time.

"I've been used to having a job because I started working when I was young," he told the BBC.

"So, when I couldn't find one it did not feel right."

When Batty appeared on BBC Breakfast to discuss his abduction, he revealed he was one of 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 not in education, employment or training.

Daniel Carolan, a manager at SUEZ UK, happened to be listening to the interview and ended up reaching out.

Carolan said: "We were talking in the office about how we can make our recruitment better and how we can find these people.

"After two minutes of listening to Alex speak I knew he was desperate to find work and I felt he deserved an opportunity."

Three months on, Batty said it was "a great feeling" knowing he was in employment.

"It was a lot of pressure when I didn't have a job because I have a family.

"You're sitting there doing everything you can but [applications] are all online and you can't show anyone what you can do."

He added: "I've got a baby and my missus, and without a job there is a pressure to support them financially.

"So it gives us security, and I know I can provide for my family."

articles.title: 'I was given electric shocks to knock the homosexuality out of my brain'
articles.summary: People who were subjected to electric shocks to change their sexuality demand the government apologises.
articles.body:
More victims of controversial electric shock therapy used to try to change their sexuality have come forward to call on the government to investigate the historical "scandal".

They spoke out after the BBC revealed that more than 260 people had been subjected to the discredited treatment at NHS hospitals in the 1960s and 1970s.

The people, who are now in their 70s and 80s, said they had been left physically and emotionally traumatised by their experiences.

And while the government said it would be drafting legislation to ban "aversion therapy", ten months on, the people spoken to by the BBC said they were still yet to receive an apology for what they had endured.

The BBC's investigation uncovered evidence that LGBT+ patients were subjected to electric shock aversion therapy in NHS hospitals across England.

Patients were shown images associated with same-sex attraction while being given painful electric shocks in an attempt to change their sexuality.

Norman Goodman, 75, said that from childhood he felt more like a girl than a boy, and told his parents that he wanted to be female.

He was admitted to a psychiatric hospital in Manchester when he was 18, in the late 1960s.

He told the BBC doctors said they would try to make it easier for him, but he was given electric shocks.

"I didn't realise it was to knock the homosexuality out of my brain," he told the BBC.

He said he was strapped to a bed and electrodes were put on his arms, legs and on either side of his head, before electricity was passed through them.

" It was absolutely terrible. They started shocking me. I was really frightened.

"And next thing I knew, it was as though I didn't know where I was.

"I didn't even know who I was. I was very weak. I had no appetite and no energy. "

Norman said he remembered NHS staff trying to make him change his mannerisms, telling him to walk and behave in a more masculine way.

But the treatment did not change who he was.

Debbie Burley told the BBC her grandfather, Arthur James Emberton, also went through electric shock therapy.

She only found out about 20 years ago what he had been through, long after he had died.

He had been a respected businessman from Cheshire, running his own cheese company.

In 1965, aged 61, he appeared at Nantwich magistrates' court after being charged with indecent assault. He had been caught kissing a boy in a doorway.

The court heard he was given probation on the condition that he sought medical treatment.

Court documents show that treatment had already begun before he was sentenced.

According to Debbie, Arthur's wife divorced him, he was forced out of the family business - which was later sold - and spent much of the rest of his life living alone in YMCA accommodation.

While the documents do not indicate what treatment he received, family members later learned he had gone through electric shock aversion therapy.

Debbie said the consequences were catastrophic.

"He never rebuilt his life," she said. "He carried that shame for the rest of his life.

"As an adult, I now understand the enormous injustice done to him," she said.

"He was wronged by the state, the medical system and the attitudes of the time."

Another man who contacted the BBC said he was 16 when he realised he was attracted to men.

"I thought I was the only one in the world," said the man, who asked to remain anonymous because, even though he is in his late 80s, he has never told his family that he is gay.

He said his parents took him to a doctor, who prescribed testosterone tablets.

But, he said, the medication made him aggressive and unwell.

So he was referred for electric shock treatment at a mental health unit.

The treatment took place once a week for about two years.

"The shock treatment itself was terrible," he said. "And after the shocks, I was like a zombie.

"I'd be going to sleep at all times of the day at home and I'd wake up crying."

Doctors told him the treatment would "straighten him out".

But, he said, it did not change the way he felt.

Most of the people who had electric shock aversion therapy were men.

But records show some women and, in some cases, children were also subjected to the treatment.

People were referred by their families, schools, churches, or the courts.

Hel Spandler, Prof of Mental health studies at the University of Lancashire, said the figure of 260 was likely to be far lower than the true number.

"Sadly, I think this figure is quite conservative and it's likely that considerably more LGBT people were affected," they said.

"We need to remember that, at the time, being gay or trans was considered a mental disorder, and this type of aversion therapy was one of many so-called therapies used to try and 'treat' it.

"While it was probably the most controversial method, for over a decade it was an accepted practice in the NHS.

"Indeed NHS hospitals in every major city in England had aversion therapy suites precisely for this purpose."

Professor Spandler said there was evidence the practice was also exported to other countries, and that hundreds more people may have undergone the treatment.

Many of those affected are now elderly, and some have spent decades carrying the trauma in silence.

They are calling not only for a full investigation into historic conversion practices, but also for accountability and a comprehensive ban on all forms of conversion therapy.

But a bill currently working its way through Parliament, the draft Conversion Practices Bill, has met with opposition from some religious groups.

The Bishop of Leicester raised in the House of Lords his concern "about the lack of clarity on the difference between harmful conversion practices and perfectly acceptable practices of pastoral care and indeed prayer".

Norman told the BBC he wanted the government to apologise for what people like him had been put through.

"I would like to see them on the television talking about what had happened to people like me. Yes, to apologize.

"I would like them to look at records from years ago, and I would like it to become more in the media so today's young people can see what happened and today's medics can learn from what had happened."

The Draft Conversion Practices Bill defines conversion practice as anything carried out with the intention of making people change, or believe that they have changed, their sexual orientation or gender identity.

The government said it "thanked everyone who has courageously come forward to share their experiences of these abhorrent historical practices".

It added: "We remain determined to ensure full transparency over the past use of electric shock aversion therapy in NHS settings.

"In the meantime, we are also taking action through our draft legislation published in June to ensure that all so-called conversion practices are banned for good."

articles.title: Eleanor Donaldson: Stormont launches review of legal framework on trials of the facts
articles.summary: The ministers will appoint an external reviewer with the review aiming to launch in late October and end by the end of February 2027.
articles.body:
Stormont's justice and health ministers have launched a joint review of the legal framework on trials of the facts in the wake of the Donaldson trial, BBC News NI understands.

That's according to a letter from the Department of Justice's assembly liaison officer.

Eleanor Donaldson, wife of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson, had faced a trial of the facts after being found unfit for a conventional trial on mental health grounds.

The ministers will appoint an external reviewer with the review aiming to launch in late October and conclude by the end of February 2027.

The letter to Stormont's justice committee said the move came in the wake of "public concern and interest" on trials of the facts, and that work would now take place on the terms of reference of the review.

Both the Department of Justice and the Department of Health have been contacted for comment.

A trial of the facts is an option that is open to prosecutors if a court determines that a person is unfit to stand trial and criminal proceedings cannot go ahead.

It takes the place of a criminal trial and is used to determine whether an accused committed the acts alleged.

It cannot result in a conviction, but if the court is not satisfied that the accused committed the acts alleged, then he/she will be acquitted.

The procedure is allowed for in legislation by Article 49A of the Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986.

The mechanism is not used often but one high-profile example was in the trial of former IRA leader Ivor Bell in 2019.

What happens during a trial of the facts?

In some ways, it is similar to a normal criminal trial - the prosecution puts its evidence against the defendant before a judge and jury in a courtroom.

However, perhaps the key difference, is that the accused does not play a part in proceedings, and does not even need to be in court.

That was the case with Eleanor Donaldson, who was not present on any day of the four-week trial in which evidence was heard against her and her husband.

However, in a trial of the facts the accused will be represented by a legal team and their lawyers can question the witnesses, challenge the evidence and make legal submissions on their behalf.

Ian Turkington KC represented Eleanor Donaldson during her trial of the facts, cross-examining witnesses and issuing closing remarks on behalf of his client towards the end of the trial.

Then there is the major differences in what the outcome can be in a trial of the facts.

Instead of being asked to return a verdict of guilty or not guilty, the jury are asked to decide whether or not the accused committed the offence with which they were charged.

The focus is on what they are alleged to have physically done - not their state of mind at the time.

In a normal criminal trial, a jury would be invited to decide whether or not a defendant had the mental faculties required to be guilty of the offence as well.

The standard of proof remains the same - a jury must be sure beyond all reasonable doubt that the accused committed the acts alleged.

The accused cannot be convicted but they can be acquitted if the jury decide they didn't commit the acts alleged.

Criminal justice and mental health provision

Solicitor Paul Dougan described a trial of the facts as a "fusion between criminal justice and mental health provision".

He said there is a "relatively high bar" with regards to medical evidence that needs to be presented, which requires oral evidence from a medical practitioner and a report from at least one further medical practitioner.

He added that people may feel a trial of the facts is "some form of lesser process" for someone who was medically unfit, which he would "argue against".

"With the involvement of medical practitioners and the interrogation of that process by a judge, at the moment it seems to me that the process is quite robust and a very high evidential threshold to be overcome.

"I would just caution people against jumping to conclusions based on a particularly high profile case that has brought these issue to the fore," Dougan said.

articles.title: 'My mother apologised': A survivor's journey after genital mutilation
articles.summary: Sara Kahsai was 29 when she found out she had FGM as a baby.
articles.body:
Sara Kahsai grew up in Sudan but moved to Birmingham, England, in 2022 after a marrying a bus driver from the city.

But as she settled into married life and her new home, she was coming to terms with a life-changing discovery.

Sara realised she was a victim-survivor of Female Genital Mutiliation (FGM), a procedure she had endured as a young girl.

She was floored by the revelation and, not least, the excruciating pain she was now beginning to fully understand.

"It made it difficult with my physical relationship with my husband - but he was very kind and very patient with me."

Warning: This story contains descriptions of the practices involved in female genital mutilation

Sara turned to the one person she knew must have orchestrated it - her mother - and asked her why.

"I was a baby. It was the culture to do it for everybody," she said her mother, still living in Africa, told her.

"When I spoke to my mum she was really upset and she apologised to me."

FGM involves the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons, and is practiced in some parts of Africa, the Middle East and Asia.

It also happens within some migrant communities in the UK, where it is illegal and treated as child abuse. It is also against the law to take a girl abroad for FGM.

Reasons include social acceptance, religion, misconceptions about hygiene and preserving a girl or woman's virginity.

The Home Office website cites World Health Organisation figures showing three million girls undergo some form of the procedure every year in Africa alone.

When Sara fell pregnant, she finally told health professionals she had endured FGM as a child.

She was immediately referred to the specialist FGM Clinic, run by midwives at Birmingham Women's Hospital.

Midwife Renata Hanif deals with around 200 cases each year and says her job is to ensure the wellbeing of women and safeguard unborn children.

"Some types of female circumcision can affect the vaginal delivery," she said.

They offer deinfibulation - a procedure that can be carried out during pregnancy that to separate fused tissue and enable safer births.

What is FGM, where does it happen and why?

Victim-survivors of FGM can also experience difficulty with urinating and menstruating, the midwife said.

Women are more prone to infections and sepsis, and can suffer from severe and ongoing pain, as well having to deal with psychological trauma, anxiety and depression.

Many patients find it hard to talk to her about what's happened to them, Hanif said.

"It is very difficult, very emotional. It's very difficult for the woman to actually come forward and to come to the clinic, attend the clinic, and have a conversation with me as well," she said.

"I explain to them that I'm here to help and I try to explain to them what happened to them when they were a child."

She said most women leave the clinic with a better understanding of how they have been affected and how they can take back control of their bodies.

"We talk about every part, what that part is there for and what's been removed and what cause for concern and what effect this will have for the rest of her life," Hanif said.

Counselling is also offered as well as information on how partners and husbands can support them.

In 2015, children's charity Barnardo's set up the National FGM Centre to help better protect women and girls.

It works to prevent FGM, raise awareness of it and support those affected.

The centre said schools are legally required to teach pupils about FGM and the law surrounding it as part of relationships and sex education.

But how it is delivered can vary between schools. It's also not mandatory for it to be taught in primary schools and they want to see that change.

"For us, a huge part of tackling FGM is prevention," Roma Ullah, from the centre, said.

"Yes, a conviction, a prosecution, can provide justice, accountability and send strong messages into communities, but by then the harm has already happened."

In April, the government held its first dedicated FGM Summit in a decade, to discuss ways to better protect women and girls.

Among improvements on the way are new guidelines to help identify girls at risk of being taken abroad for FGM.

Sara wants to urge other women in a similar position to take immediate action.

"I have a message to all ladies who've had FGM," she said.

"When they come to the UK it is different. There's help here - go to their GP, seek help, ask for help.

"If I knew I could seek help I would not have waited until I was expecting... because I did suffer a lot before."

articles.title: Coventry tourism tops £1bn for first time
articles.summary: Food, shopping and events help drive a record year for Coventry, tourism bosses say.
articles.body:
Tourism bosses in Coventry say a landmark year for the city has seen visitor spending generate more than £1bn in economic value for the first time.

New figures show 12.6 million people visited the city in 2025, up 6.5% on the previous year.

Destination Coventry said the growth coincided with a year that included part of Coventry City's Championship-winning season and major concerts at the CBS Arena featuring Ed Sheeran, Bob Dylan and Tom Grennan.

Pete Chambers, director of the Coventry Music Museum, said he had noticed visitors travelling from further afield.

"We get people from all over the world. We've had people from, I think, 103 different countries," he said.

"Nearly 60,000 people [have visited the museum] and a lot of those are from Australia, America, New Zealand and Africa.

"I just think it's going to get better and better."

Paul McMahon, managing director of Destination Coventry, said the figures reflected years of work by businesses and organisations across the city.

"It's an absolute endorsement of the incredible amount of hard work done over a number of years by every single business and every single individual that works in the city," he said.

Sue Pinn, who was visiting from Exeter, said she had been encouraged by a friend to visit Coventry Indoor Market.

"I was told I had to go for the smells and the variety of different foods," she said.

"It's fabulous. I could have wandered around all day. Some of the food I didn't recognise, just brilliant."

Ted and Lynn Walker, from Cumbria, were visiting Coventry as part of a holiday in Stratford-upon-Avon.

The couple said they made a point of visiting the city whenever they were in the area.

"Beautiful, we love Coventry," Walker said.

"Every time we come to Stratford, we catch the X18 bus and have a look around the cathedral, do a little shopping and it's just absolutely wonderful."

The figures were calculated using the STEAM (Scarborough Tourism Economic Activity Monitor) model, allowing comparisons with other destinations.

Destination Coventry said visitor spending supported 8,330 full-time jobs in the city during 2025.

There was also a large rise in people using non-serviced accommodation, such as Airbnb properties and rented accommodation, increasing by 14.3%.

Food and drink accounted for 33% of tourism spending in the city, while shopping made up 29%.

Recreation, including spending on museums, galleries and events, accounted for 11%.

Lynnette Kelly, Coventry City Council's cabinet member for jobs, regeneration and climate change, said the figures demonstrated the importance of tourism to the local economy.

"Reaching this milestone reflects the strength and diversity of what the city has to offer, with our attractions, events, hospitality and cultural experiences all contributing to a thriving visitor economy," she said.

McMahon said he expected visitor numbers to continue growing.

"There are a lot of events happening, both in leisure and the business world, and I think we'll be in a good place over the coming years," he said.

articles.body: MUMBAI: Disha Salian’s father, Satish Salian, has sent a defamation notice seeking Rs 500 crore in compensation from Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray and former Maharashtra home minister Anil Deshmukh over statements concerning his daughter’s death.The notice demands that the two leaders apologise, retract the statements and pay Rs 500 crore in compensation. They have been given seven days to comply with the demands.The notice comes after Thackeray on Wednesday denied ever meeting Salian, who was the former manager of actor Sushant Singh Rajput, and said attempts to link his name to her death were part of a “false campaign”.In a post on X, Thackeray said he had “never met Disha Salian” and had no acquaintance with her. He alleged that his name had been linked to the case repeatedly for the past six years for “political motives” and out of “personal enmity”."I have never met Disha Salian, nor did I have any acquaintance with her. For political motives, out of personal enmity, with the intent of character assassination, for the past 6 years, some people have been deliberately trying to link my name to this unfortunate incident repeatedly, despite there being no evidence or connection whatsoever.""This constant false campaign, devoid of any facts or truth, is unfortunate. The false discussions on TV channels and media trials carried out through empty bluster cannot alter the truth. Allow the official machinery to conduct this inquiry afresh—without any interference, without political intervention, without character assassination, and impartially," he added.CBI registers FIRThe notice comes days after the Central Bureau of Investigation registered an FIR in connection with Salian’s death on September 14, following a direction from the Bombay High Court for a thorough probe.Advocate Nilesh Ojha, who represents Satish Salian, said on Monday that the FIR names Thackeray, Rohan Roy, Rhea Chakraborty, Param Bir Singh, Dino Morea, Sooraj Pancholi and then DCP Vishal Thakur, among others.The FIR also names the police inspector of Malwani police station, members of the Special Investigation Team, a doctor and a chemical analyst, according to Ojha.Salian, who had worked as Sushant Singh Rajput’s manager, died in Mumbai in June 2020 after falling from a building. articles.title: India and Pakistan summon diplomats after ships collide in international waters
articles.summary: Both sides accuse each other of causing the collision which happened in the Arabian Sea on Tuesday.
articles.body:
India and Pakistan have summoned each other's top diplomats in Delhi and Islamabad after two of their naval vessels collided in the Arabian Sea.

Both sides blamed each other for the collision, which happened on Tuesday. They also accused each other of violating a 1991 bilateral agreement that requires either side to give advance notice of military exercises.

While India said the incident did not cause any major damage, the statement released by Pakistan did not make clear whether its vessel was damaged in any way.

The incident comes more than a year after the South Asian neighbours conducted military strikes against each other before agreeing on a ceasefire.

In its statement, India said it had lodged a strong protest with the Charge d'Affaires of the Pakistani High Commission in Delhi over what it called "unacceptable and unprofessional conduct" of the naval unit.

"The Charge d'Affaires of Pakistan was advised to convey to the concerned Pakistani authorities, the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents," India's external affairs ministry said.

On the same day, Pakistan also summoned India's Charge d'Affaires in Islamabad, lodging its complaint against what it called a "highly provocative and unacceptable" action by India's naval vessel.

In its statement, Pakistan's foreign affairs ministry said that its navy was conducting its biennial exercise, SEASPARK-26, in its exclusive economic zone when the Indian vessel "carried out aggressive manoeuvres in dangerously close proximity" of its ship.

Pakistan also urged the international community to call upon India to "refrain from irresponsible actions that could further destabilise South Asia", saying that the region could not afford to be held "hostage to India's reckless pursuit of conflict and instability".

The Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troops Movements - which both sides accuse the other of violating - was signed in 1991 to prevent "any crisis situation arising due to misreading of the other side's intentions".

India specifically accused Pakistan of violating Article 10 of the agreement, which says that the two countries' naval vessels and submarines must not be closer than three nautical miles from each other so as to avoid accidents while operating in international waters.

articles.title: Thailand grew rubber trees on the same land for 75 years; scientists found soil biodiversity deteriorated after repeated plantation cycles
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Thailand’s rubber industry has relied on the same land for generations, but scientists have found that repeated planting may come at the expense of th.
articles.body: Thailand’s rubber industry has relied on the same land for generations, but scientists have found that repeated planting may come at the expense of the surface. Rubber plantations in southern Thailand found that soil biodiversity declined as rubber was replanted through successive rotations, with the sharpest deterioration appearing in the third rotation. Because a typical rubber plantation lasts about 25 years, three rotations can represent roughly 75 years of continuous rubber production. The researchers found that the soil biodiversity quality index deteriorated after about 50 years, suggesting that prolonged monocropping can gradually weaken the biological health of the soil.Repeated rubber planting damaged soil biodiversityAccording to the study published in the Journal of Taylor and Francis, titled ‘How 75 years of rubber monocropping affects soil fauna and nematodes as the bioindicators for soil biodiversity quality index’, the rubber trees studied were Hevea brasiliensis, the main commercial source of natural rubber. In the area, the original rubber plantations were established after forests were cleared. The researchers noted that Thailand's rubber-growing areas have commonly gone through two or three replanting cycles, while the typical economic lifespan of a rubber plantation is around 25 years. This means the same piece of land can remain under rubber production for decades, with new trees planted after earlier plantations reach the end of their productive lives.To examine what happened over those repeated cycles, the scientists compared an adjacent natural forest with rubber plantations representing three rotations. Each rotation was assessed at both an early stage, between three and six years old, and an old stage, between 18 and 22 years old. The study therefore compared forest with first-, second- and third-rotation rubber plantations rather than simply looking at one plantation over 75 years. Soil samples were taken from the top 10 centimetres, where much of the soil biota responsible for soil processes is found.Soil animals revealed biodiversity lossThey examined soil macrofauna and nematodes as indicators of soil biodiversity. 30 macrofaunal taxonomic groups were identified and placed into feeding categories, including predators, detritivores, phytophagous organisms, omnivores and geophagous organisms. Earthworms were particularly relevant because they belong to the geophagous group and can influence soil structure and the movement of water and gases through the soil.Nematodes provided another window into the soil food web. Bacterivorous nematodes were the most abundant feeding group in the study, but their numbers were highest in the forest and declined in old rubber plantations. The same downward pattern was found for omnivorous and plant-parasitic nematodes, as well as total nematode abundance and richness. Nematode richness continued to fall along the rubber chronosequence, reaching its lowest level in the old stage of the third rotation.The third rubber rotation showed the greatest soil declineThe researchers combined seven measurements of soil macrofauna and nematodes into a biodiversity quality index. This included measures such as predator and earthworm-group abundance, macrofaunal richness, and several nematode measures. The resulting index decreased significantly along the succession of rubber plantations and reached its lowest value in the third rotation. Nematode richness was identified as the main driver of the biodiversity index in this study, followed by earthworm abundance.The researchers also found that soil chemical properties followed a broadly similar pattern. Soil fertility decreased immediately after deforestation and land-use change, while potassium, magnesium and calcium decreased after deforestation and successive rotations. The study reported that soil degradation was evident in the third rotation. Importantly, the biodiversity quality index did not show a difference between the first and second rotations, but it was considerably reduced in the third.Soil damage built up after decades of rubberThe findings suggest that the damage associated with continuous rubber monocropping builds over time rather than appearing only when a plantation is first established. The researchers observed a rapid decline in soil properties and biodiversity immediately after forest clearance, followed by continued deterioration along the rubber chronosequence. They linked this pattern to changes in habitat, soil organic carbon and nutrient availability following land-use conversion and repeated plantation disturbance.Although three 25-year plantation cycles amount to roughly 75 years of potential rubber production, the researchers concluded that soil biodiversity quality had deteriorated after the second rotation, at about 50 years of continuous rubber monocropping. They suggested that two rotations appeared to be the maximum period for rubber monocropping in terms of soil biodiversity recovery, and pointed to agroforestry or intercropping as alternative approaches that could help maintain environmental benefits.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
